content: <example_question> What is free cash flow and why is it important? </example_question>

<example_answer> Free Cash Flow (FCF) measures cash available after capital expenditures. Formula: FCF = Operating Cash Flow − Capital Expenditures. It is designed to assess cash generation available for debt repayment, dividends, or reinvestment. Higher FCF may suggest financial flexibility. FCF does not capture financing flows and may fluctuate due to investment cycles. It assumes capital expenditures are appropriately classified. It is often complemented by EBITDA and net income to compare accrual and cash performance. Data come from the cash flow statement. For example, $20m operating cash flow and $8m capex yield $12m FCF. </example_answer>

<example_answer> EBITDA Margin measures operating performance before non-cash and financing effects. Formula: EBITDA Margin = EBITDA / Revenue. It is designed to approximate operating cash generation before capital structure and accounting differences. A higher margin may suggest operational strength. It excludes capital expenditures and working capital needs, potentially overstating cash generation. It varies by capital intensity and industry. It is often complemented by FCF and operating margin for fuller analysis. Data include EBITDA (income statement adjustments) and revenue. For example, $15m EBITDA on $60m revenue implies 25%. </example_answer>

<example_answer> Asset Turnover measures revenue generated per unit of assets. Formula: Asset Turnover = Revenue / Average Total Assets. It is designed to assess asset utilization efficiency. A higher ratio may suggest effective use of assets, while a lower ratio could indicate underutilization. It does not measure profitability and varies significantly by industry. It assumes assets are properly valued. It is often complemented by profit margins to decompose ROA (DuPont analysis). Data come from income statement and balance sheet. For example, $200m revenue and $100m assets imply 2.0 turnover. </example_answer>
